paragraphs: Miüsov was a man of breeding and delicacy, and he could not help feeling some inward qualms as he reached the Father Superior’s with Ivan. He was ashamed of having lost his temper. He felt he should have despised that contemptible wretch Fyodor Pavlovitch too much to be upset by him in Father Zossima’s cell and forget himself like that. “The monks were not to blame, in any case,” he reflected on the steps. “And if they’re decent people here (and the Father Superior, I understand, is a nobleman), why not be friendly and courteous with them? I won’t argue. I’ll go along with everything. I’ll win them over by politeness, and ... and ... show them that I have nothing to do with that Æsop, that buffoon, that Pierrot, and have simply been taken in over this affair, just as they have.”

He decided to drop his lawsuit against the monastery and give up his claims to the wood-cutting and fishing rights at once. He was all the readier to do this because the rights had become much less valuable, and he had only the vaguest idea where the wood and river in question were.

These excellent intentions grew stronger when he entered the Father Superior’s dining room. Strictly speaking, it was not a dining room, since the Father Superior had only two rooms in all. They were, however, much larger and more comfortable than Father Zossima’s. But there was no great luxury in the furnishing of these rooms either. The furniture was mahogany, upholstered in leather, in the old-fashioned style of 1820. The floor was not even stained, but everything shone with cleanliness, and there were many choice flowers in the windows. The most sumptuous thing in the room at that moment was, of course, the beautifully laid table. The cloth was clean and the dishes gleamed. There were three kinds of well-baked bread, two bottles of wine, two of excellent mead, and a large glass jug of kvas. The mead and the kvas were both made in the monastery and famous in the neighborhood. There was no vodka. Rakitin related afterwards that there were five dishes: fish soup made of sterlets, served with little fish patties; then boiled fish served in a special way; then salmon cutlets, ice pudding and compote; and finally, blanc-mange. Rakitin found out about all these good things because he could not resist peeping into the kitchen, where he already had a foothold. He had a foothold everywhere and got information about everything. He was of an uneasy and envious temper. He was well aware of his own considerable abilities and nervously exaggerated them in his self-conceit. He knew he would play some prominent part, but Alyosha, who was attached to him, was distressed to see that his friend Rakitin was dishonorable and quite unconscious of it himself. On the contrary, he considered that because he would not steal money left lying on the table, he was a man of the highest integrity. Neither Alyosha nor anyone else could have changed his mind about that.

Rakitin, of course, was too unimportant a person to be invited to the dinner. The only monks invited were Father Iosif, Father Païssy and one other. They were already waiting when Miüsov, Kalganov and Ivan arrived. The other guest, Maximov, stood a little to one side, waiting too. The Father Superior stepped into the middle of the room to receive his guests. He was a tall, thin but still vigorous old man, with black hair streaked with gray and a long, grave, ascetic face. He bowed to his guests in silence. This time they went up to receive his blessing. Miüsov even tried to kiss his hand, but the Father Superior drew it back in time to avoid the kiss. Ivan and Kalganov, though, went through the ceremony in the simplest and most complete way, kissing his hand as peasants do.

“We must apologize most humbly, your reverence,” Miüsov began, simpering affably and speaking in a dignified, respectful tone. “Forgive us for coming without the gentleman you invited, Fyodor Pavlovitch. He felt obliged to decline the honor of your hospitality, and not without reason. In the reverend Father Zossima’s cell he was carried away by the unhappy quarrel with his son and let fall some words that were quite out of keeping ... in fact, quite improper ... as”—he glanced at the monks—“your reverence is, no doubt, already aware. And so, recognizing that he was to blame, he felt sincere regret and shame, and asked me and his son Ivan Fyodorovitch to convey to you his apologies and regrets. In short, he hopes and intends to make amends later. He asks your blessing and begs you to forget what has happened.”
As he spoke the last word of his tirade, Miüsov recovered his self-satisfaction completely, and every trace of his earlier irritation vanished. He loved humanity again, fully and sincerely.
The Father Superior listened to him with dignity and, with a slight bow of the head, replied:
“I sincerely regret his absence. Perhaps at our table he might have learned to like us, and we him. Please be seated, gentlemen.”
He stood before the holy image and began to say grace aloud. All bowed their heads reverently, and Maximov clasped his hands in front of him with particular fervor.

It was at this moment that Fyodor Pavlovitch played his last prank. It must be noted that he really had meant to go home. He really had felt it was impossible to go and dine with the Father Superior as though nothing had happened, after his disgraceful behavior in the elder’s cell. Not that he was so very ashamed of himself—quite the contrary, perhaps. But still, he felt it would be improper to go to dinner. Yet his creaking carriage had hardly been brought to the steps of the hotel, and he had hardly got into it, when he suddenly stopped short. He remembered his own words at the elder’s: “I always feel when I meet people that I am lower than all of them, and that they all take me for a buffoon. So I say, let me play the buffoon, for you are, every one of you, stupider and lower than I.” He longed to take revenge on everyone for his own improper behavior. He suddenly recalled how he had once been asked, “Why do you hate so-and-so so much?” And he had answered, with his shameless impudence, “I’ll tell you. He has done me no harm. But I played him a dirty trick, and ever since I have hated him.”

Remembering that now, he smiled quietly and spitefully, hesitating for a moment. His eyes gleamed, and his lips positively quivered. “Well, since I’ve begun, I may as well go on,” he decided. The feeling uppermost in him at that moment could be put into these words: “Well, there’s no rehabilitating myself now. So let me shame them for all I’m worth. I’ll show them I don’t care what they think—that’s all!”

He told the coachman to wait, and with quick steps went back to the monastery and straight to the Father Superior’s. He had no clear idea what he would do, but he knew that he could not control himself and that a mere touch might drive him to the utmost limits of obscenity—but only to obscenity, to nothing criminal, nothing for which he could be punished by law. In the last resort, he could always restrain himself, and had sometimes marveled at himself on that score. He appeared in the Father Superior’s dining room just as the prayer ended and everyone was moving to the table. Standing in the doorway, he looked the company over and, laughing his long, impudent, spiteful chuckle, looked them all boldly in the face. “They thought I’d gone, and here I am again,” he cried to the whole room.

For one moment everyone stared at him without a word, and at once everyone felt that something revolting, grotesque, positively scandalous was about to happen. Miüsov went immediately from the most benevolent frame of mind to the most savage. All the feelings that had subsided and died down in his heart revived instantly.
“No! This I cannot endure!” he cried. “I absolutely cannot! And ... I certainly cannot!”
The blood rushed to his head. He positively stammered, but he was past thinking about style, and he seized his hat.
“What is it he cannot?” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. “What is it he absolutely cannot and certainly cannot? Your reverence, am I to come in or not? Will you receive me as your guest?”

“You are welcome with all my heart,” answered the Superior. “Gentlemen!” he added, “I venture to ask you most earnestly to lay aside your quarrels and be united in love and family harmony—with prayer to the Lord at our humble table.”
“No, no, it’s impossible!” cried Miüsov, beside himself.

“Well, if it’s impossible for Pyotr Alexandrovitch, it’s impossible for me, and I won’t stay. That’s why I came. I’ll keep with Pyotr Alexandrovitch everywhere now. If you go away, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, I’ll go away too. If you stay, I’ll stay. You stung him with what you said about family harmony, Father Superior. He doesn’t admit he’s my relation. That’s right, isn’t it, von Sohn? Here’s von Sohn. How are you, von Sohn?”
“Do you mean me?” muttered Maximov, puzzled.
“Of course I mean you,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. “Who else? The Father Superior can’t be von Sohn.”
“But I’m not von Sohn either. I’m Maximov.”

“No, you’re von Sohn. Your reverence, do you know who von Sohn was? It was a famous murder case. He was killed in a house of harlotry—I believe that’s what such places are called among you—he was killed and robbed, and in spite of his venerable age, he was nailed up in a box and sent from Petersburg to Moscow in the luggage van. And while they were nailing him up, the harlots sang songs and played the harp, that is to say, the piano. So this is that very von Sohn. He has risen from the dead, hasn’t he, von Sohn?”
“What’s going on? What’s this?” voices were heard among the monks.
“Let’s go,” cried Miüsov, speaking to Kalganov.

“No, excuse me,” Fyodor Pavlovitch broke in shrilly, taking another step into the room. “Let me finish. In the cell you blamed me for behaving disrespectfully just because I spoke of eating gudgeon, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. Miüsov, my relation, prefers to have _plus de noblesse que de sincérité_ in his words, but I prefer in mine _plus de sincérité que de noblesse_, and—damn the _noblesse_! That’s right, isn’t it, von Sohn? Allow me, Father Superior. I am a buffoon and I play the buffoon, but I am the soul of honor, and I want to speak my mind. Yes, I am the soul of honor, while in Pyotr Alexandrovitch there is wounded vanity and nothing else. I came here, perhaps, to have a look and speak my mind. My son Alexey is here, being saved. I am his father. I care for his welfare, and it’s my duty to care. While I’ve been playing the fool, I’ve been listening and having a look on the sly. And now I want to give you the last act of the performance. You know how things are with us? As a thing falls, so it lies. Once a thing has fallen, it must lie there for ever. Not a bit of it! I want to get up again. Holy Father, I am indignant with you. Confession is a great sacrament, and I’m ready to bow down before it reverently. But there in the cell they all kneel down and confess aloud. Can it be right to confess aloud? The holy Fathers ordained that confession be made in secret. Only then is your confession a mystery, and so it was of old. But how can I explain to him in front of everyone that I did this and that ... well, you understand what—sometimes it wouldn’t be proper to talk about it—so it’s really a scandal! No, Fathers, a man might be carried along with you into the Flagellants, I suppose ... at the first opportunity I’ll write to the Synod, and I’ll take my son Alexey home.”
